title: How Yo-Yos Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how yo-yos work, covering the etymology of "yo," the toy's history from ancient hunting weapons and early European designs through the Filipino design, Pedro Flores, Donald Duncan and the Duncan company's trademark loss and move to Luck, Wisconsin, and the physics of linear momentum, angular momentum, gyroscopic stability, and moment of inertia. They discuss sleeping and walking the dog, ball-bearing and clutch yo-yos (the "Yo-Yo with the Brain"), NASA's zero-gravity yo-yo test, and a few trivia items (Abbie Hoffman's HUAC contempt charge, Nixon at the Grand Ole Opry). The episode ends with a listener mail about a charity compilation album for Japan earthquake relief.

segments.title: Opening banter and Harlem Nights
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about backaches and tease the episode. They discuss the movie Harlem Nights and Eddie Murphy's use of the word 'yo' in a 1920s setting, and Josh says 'yo' was in use in the 1920s, originating as a hunting cry and sailor call before the modern usage from Philadelphia's Italian quarters after World War II.

segments.title: Early history of the yo-yo
segments.summary: The hosts discuss early yo-yo forms: the older design with the string tied tight to the axle, found in ancient Greece, China and Europe, with names such as the lemniscate, bandalore and the hoop-and-stick. They mention Napoleon's use of a yo-yo for stress relief. The Filipino design, in which the string loops loosely around the axle, led to the modern yo-yo and lets it spin at the end of the string.

segments.title: Filipino hunting weapon and Duncan company history
segments.summary: The yo-yo was a large hunting weapon in the Philippines before becoming a toy. Pedro Flores, a Filipino immigrant, started a US yo-yo company in the 1920s and sold it to Donald Duncan, who kept the yo-yo name. Competitors challenged the trademark and federal courts ruled in the 1960s that the name was generic. Legal battles contributed to the Duncan company's bankruptcy. The company moved to Luck, Wisconsin in the 1940s and at its peak made many yo-yos an hour; it sold 45 million yo-yos in 1962. June 6 is National Yo-Yo Day, Donald Duncan's birthday.

segments.title: Physics: linear and angular momentum, gyroscopic stability
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that a yo-yo has linear momentum as it moves up and down and angular momentum as it spins on its axle. The angular momentum builds as it falls, which keeps it spinning ('sleeping'). Gyroscopic stability means a spinning object resists changes to its axis of rotation, which is why the yo-yo returns after a push. They compare this to a football spiral and a wobbling throw.

segments.title: Moment of inertia and yo-yo design changes
segments.summary: The hosts explain moment of inertia as a spinning object's resistance to changes in rotation. Adding mass further from the axis increases it, which is why inverted, butterfly-style yo-yos from Duncan were designed as they were, and the design changes in the 1960s added outer mass and extended axles. Josh references a Murphy's Law book pun.

segments.title: Ball-bearing and clutch yo-yos
segments.summary: The ball-bearing yo-yo splits the axle into inner and outer races separated by ball bearings, so the outer race spins the inner race and the yo-yo can sleep longer. The clutch-based Yo-Yo with the Brain, released by Yomega in the 1990s and designed by Michael Caffrey, uses spring-loaded clutch arms that engage and disengage based on centrifugal force, so the yo-yo spins for a time and then re-engages to return. Tom Kuhn's No Jive yo-yo is also mentioned.

segments.title: Trivia: Abbie Hoffman, Nixon, NASA zero-gravity test
segments.summary: The hosts recount Abbie Hoffman being charged with contempt of Congress when he yo-yoed during a House Un-American Activities Committee session. They describe Nixon's awkward attempt at a yo-yo at the Grand Ole Opry, and a NASA test in which a yo-yo was spun in microgravity, where it would not sleep. The hosts note the test was part of the Toys in Space project.

segments.title: Closing banter and search tip
segments.summary: The hosts wrap the physics discussion and share a tip on using minus signs in search queries to filter results, then point listeners to the HowStuffWorks yo-yo article. Chuck mentions an unrelated jewelry store encounter with the rapper Neo.

segments.title: Listener mail: Japan earthquake charity album
segments.summary: A listener named Anna writes about the charity compilation More Hope for Japan, with 37 tracks by 37 artists raising funds for continued earthquake and nuclear disaster relief. Her band New Century Classics contributed a new track. The hosts encourage listeners to send in suggestions for raising awareness of neglected causes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a reminder about contacting the show and a promotional note for the HowStuffWorks iPhone app.
